fields.features_heading: What the Request Has to Tell IT
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the IT request form, the routing behind it, and the queue your team works through, from a plain-English description.
fields.feature_1:
Questions that follow the request type

Pick hardware and the form asks for the asset tag and where the device sits. Pick software and it asks for the product and its yearly cost, then how many people need a seat.
fields.feature_2:
Priority set by who is stuck

The form asks whether the requester can keep working and how many others are affected. A problem that stops a whole team is marked High and lands at the front of the queue.
fields.feature_3:
Purchases wait for the budget owner

A request that costs money goes by email to its budget owner along with the quoted price and the requester's reason. IT starts the work only after that person approves.
fields.feature_4:
Requesters see where things stand

The app emails the requester when the request is assigned, when IT needs more detail, and when it closes. Nobody has to reply to an old thread to ask whether anyone saw it.
fields.feature_5:
A queue kept in a database you own

Every request is a row in a database you own, stamped with its priority and the day it came in. Sort it by age or filter it by department, with no cap on how many it holds.
fields.feature_6:
Your code, in your GitHub repository

On paid plans, export the full codebase to your GitHub repository and host it next to your other internal tools. Keep building on it in your own editor after the export.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Places an IT Request Starts
fields.tab_content_1:
From a new-hire request, three setup tasks with owners

Strand Ohlsen Architects hires Nadia Ruane as a junior designer. Nine days before she starts, her manager files a new-hire request with her role and software. The form opens a task with an owner for the laptop, the email account, and the drafting license. IT lead Amadou Sarr sees 2 done and the license still open.
fields.tab_content_2:
On a $2,400 tool, the budget owner decides before IT

Vashti Kessel runs dispatch at Haverlund Freight and asks for a route-planning tool at $2,400 a year for 6 dispatchers. Any software over $1,000 a year goes by email to the budget owner first. Here that is Brennan Okwuosa, who gets the quote and her reason. IT reviews how the tool signs people in after he approves.
fields.tab_content_3:
In Room 114, a blank screen goes to the campus tech first

The projector in Room 114 at Tamarind Middle School shows no signal mid-lesson. Marlo Eskridge reports it from her phone and sets the impact to "Class stopped," which makes the request High. Campus tech Luis Pacheco gets an alert, and the request sits above every Normal one in his queue.
fields.tab_content_4:
For the Monday review, the 6 oldest requests come first

Kittredge Community College's IT team has 37 open requests this week: 14 software, 11 hardware, 8 access, and 4 other. The 6 open longer than 5 business days sit at the top of the list, oldest first, each with its owner's name. The team's Monday review starts there and works down.

fields.howto_title: How to Create an IT Request Form
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan an IT request form around the requests your team gets, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Give each type its own questions
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask about impact in plain words
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Name an owner for each type
fields.howto_step_1_des: Read through a month of IT emails and chat messages before you add a field. Group them into the four or five types you see most, such as hardware, software, access, and help. Each type becomes a choice at the top of the form.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Ask only what IT needs to act on each type. A broken device needs the exact error message and when it started. A software request needs the business reason. Access to a system needs the system name and who signs off on it. Leave out anything IT can look up.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Skip the priority dropdown that everyone sets to Urgent. Ask whether the problem stops one person or a whole team, and let that answer set the priority. A whole office offline then outranks one slow laptop.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Decide who picks up each type and who has to say yes before any money is spent. Write the spending threshold down as a dollar amount. A request type with no named owner is the one that sits unassigned for a week.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Tell the requester what to expect
fields.howto_step_5_des: Show a request number on the confirmation screen, along with the response time your team aims for on that type, such as same day for High. Put the same number in every email about the request.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Describe it to Emergent and test it
fields.howto_step_6_des: Paste your request types and their owners into one prompt, and Emergent builds the whole app from it. Then submit five real requests from last month and check that each lands with the right person at the right priority.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Once a month, look at the requests filed as Other and the ones that stayed open longest. A cluster in Other is a request type waiting to be added. Describe the change to Emergent and it updates the form.

faq_plan.q: What is an IT request form?
faq_plan.a: An IT request form is how employees ask the IT team for something: new hardware, a software license, access to a system, or help with a problem. It records who is asking and how urgent the need is. IT assigns each request from that record and closes it there.

faq_plan.q: How do I create an IT request form?
faq_plan.a: Describe it to Emergent's AI form builder: the request types you handle, the questions each one needs, who owns each type, and who approves purchases. Emergent builds the form and the database behind it, and you change any part by prompting. The free tier covers building and publishing.

faq_plan.q: What should an IT request form template include?
faq_plan.a: Start with the fields every request shares: the requester's name and department, a request type, a description, the impact on their work, and a date they need it by. Each type then adds its own fields, such as the system name for access. Keep the shared part short and let the type decide the rest.

faq_plan.q: Can I reuse the approval steps from my IT request form for other requests?
faq_plan.a: Yes. A request type, an approver chosen by amount, and a status the requester can see carry over to other request forms. A refund request form, for example, can send any refund over a set amount to a manager before it is paid. In Emergent, you describe the new form and its approval rule in a prompt.

faq_plan.q: Should an IT request form handle incidents as well as service requests?
faq_plan.a: It can, as long as the form tells the two apart. Ask up front whether something is broken or needed, and send each kind to its own owner. Atlassian's ITSM guide calls a service request "a formal request from a user for something to be provided" and an incident "an unplanned disruption to a service."

faq_plan.q: How do I set priority levels on an IT request form?
faq_plan.a: Set priority from the answers instead of a dropdown the requester picks. Map each impact to a level: one person slowed down is Low, one person blocked is Normal, and a team or a customer-facing service blocked is High. Write the levels on the form itself, and revisit the mapping after a month of real requests.

faq_plan.q: Should requests for assistive technology go on the IT request form?
faq_plan.a: Not the request itself. An employee asking for assistive technology as a workplace accommodation should use the reasonable accommodation request form that HR handles. Once HR approves it, IT gets a setup request on the IT request form that names the software or device to install, without the reason behind it.

faq_plan.q: Is an online IT request form better than one sent by email?
faq_plan.a: Yes, for anything IT has to track. An IT request form PDF has to be filled in and emailed, and then someone retypes it into a queue before work starts. An online form puts each request straight into a database with its priority and owner. With Emergent, that database is one you own, with no response caps.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should an IT request form have?
faq_plan.a: Keep the shared part to about five questions that every request needs. Each type then adds two or three of its own. Every question beyond that should change what IT does next, and any question that does not can come off the form.

faq_plan.q: Should facilities problems go on the IT request form?
faq_plan.a: No. A stuck door or a leaking ceiling belongs on a maintenance request form that facilities owns. Keep the IT request form for devices, software, accounts, and networks. If people mix them up, add a line under the request types that points to the right form, and have IT pass misfiled requests to facilities.

plan.angle: The top 10 is template galleries (Jotform, Fluent Forms, Wufoo), a help desk blog listicle, university and county PDF or Word forms, a Reddit thread and a Scribd upload. Each one stops at a box for describing the problem. This page shows what IT does after a request lands: questions that change with the request type, priority set from how many people are stuck, purchases held for the budget owner, a weekly queue review that puts the oldest requests first, and every request kept as a row in a database the team owns. The FAQ answers the template, priority, incident and routing questions people building one ask.

findings.quote: Four Places an IT Request Starts
findings.issue: The heading says each tab is a place a request starts, and tab 4 contradicts it: 'Queue Review' is Kittredge Community College's Monday review of 37 already-open requests, not where a request starts. A heading one tab contradicts is an untrue statement about the page's own content (SEVERITY: untrue). No other tab or section heading has this defect; tabs 1-3 do start a request (a manager, a dispatcher, a teacher).
findings.fix: Retitle the section so it holds all four tabs, e.g. 'Four IT Requests, From Filing to Review' or 'Who Files IT Requests, and Who Works Them' (48 chars max, no sibling primary), or replace tab 4 with a fourth starting point; keep the tab copy and images as they are if the heading changes.
